questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presented with acutely altered mental status. The patient’s family reported that the patient had been confused for 1–2 days and had been walking into walls. He had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and poor dentition. He had no known drug allergies. Physical exam revealed mild left hemiparesis and decreased left temporal visual field. Investigations: Total white cell count 13,300 cells/mm3 Serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL Normal liver function tests MRI brain: 4 ×3 cm rim-enhancing lesion in the right parieto-occipital region. The patient was taken to the operating room, where frank pus was drained from the mass. Gram-stain of the abscess fluid: abundant gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains on direct microscopy; culture revealed viridans group streptococci.
questions.lead_in: What beta-lactam would be most appropriate to include in this patient’s antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone Cefazolin does not adequately penetrate the blood–brain barrier and is not appropriate for treatment of central nervous system infections. Cefepime and ceftazidime are established treatments for gram-negative central nervous system infections but offer no advantage over ceftriaxone for coverage of viridans group streptococci. Cefotetan is not established for treatment of central nervous system infections. Ceftriaxone is considered a therapy of choice for central nervous system infections caused by viridans group streptococcus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q6

questions.question: Female with 2 day onset of fever and headaches. [image-based question: MRI brain shown, otherwise well patient, appeared to be a R temporal lobe lesion (?brain abscess)]

parts.text: How would you make the diagnosis and what would you request from microbiology?
How would you treat (regimen and dose)?

questions.model_answer:
Diagnosis: MRI with contrast (ring-enhancing lesion with restricted diffusion on DWI is characteristic of pyogenic abscess vs. tumour); obtain blood cultures, CSF analysis only if imaging shows no risk of herniation, and neurosurgical stereotactic aspiration or excision of the lesion (>2.5 cm should be excised/aspirated) with specimens sent to microbiology for Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic culture, and to pathology for histopathology; request from microbiology: Gram stain and aerobic + anaerobic culture (plus AFB and fungal stains/culture if immunocompromised or risk factors present).
Treatment (unclear pathogenesis/empiric, unknown source): vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h, trough/AUC-guided) + metronidazole (7.5 mg/kg IV q6h or 500 mg IV q8h) + a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h or cefepime 2 g IV q8h if Pseudomonas suspected), then narrow based on culture and source.

questions.question: Frontal brain abscess

parts.text: Empiric therapy
Where did this abscess come from

questions.model_answer:
a) Empiric therapy: metronidazole + third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime); add vancomycin if MRSA/S. aureus is a concern.
b) Source: paranasal sinuses (frontoethmoid/frontal sinusitis).

questions.question: Question on brain abscess.

parts.text: List the ways infection can reach the brain (and associated bacteria)
Recommend empiric treatment for each of the above, based on expected bacteriology (list abx/antifungals that don't cross the BBB)
List indications for surgical intervention/evacuation
List indications for MRSA and Pseudomonas coverage in brain infections
List organisms associated with concurrent Brain/Lung infections and their treatment

questions.model_answer:
a) Routes to the brain and associated bacteria: (1) Contiguous spread - otitis media/mastoiditis (streptococci, Bacteroides/Prevotella, Enterobacteriaceae), sinusitis (streptococci, Bacteroides spp., Enterobacteriaceae, S. aureus, Haemophilus spp.), dental infection (Fusobacterium, Prevotella, Actinomyces, Bacteroides, streptococci); (2) Hematogenous spread - from lung abscess/empyema/bronchiectasis (Fusobacterium, Actinomyces, streptococci), endocarditis (S. aureus, viridans streptococci), congenital cyanotic heart disease (streptococci); (3) Direct inoculation - penetrating trauma or post-neurosurgery (S. aureus, streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium spp.).
b) Empiric treatment by source: Otitis media/mastoiditis, sinusitis, dental infection - metronidazole + 3rd-gen cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime); Penetrating trauma/postneurosurgical - vancomycin + 3rd/4th-gen cephalosporin; Lung abscess/empyema/bronchiectasis source - 3rd-gen cephalosporin + metronidazole + a sulfonamide (for Nocardia coverage); Endocarditis - vancomycin; Congenital heart disease - 3rd-gen cephalosporin alone; Unknown source - vancomycin + metronidazole + 3rd/4th-gen cephalosporin. (Antimicrobials that do not cross the blood-brain barrier well and should be avoided/are unreliable for CNS infection include first-generation cephalosporins, macrolides, and clindamycin.)
c) Indications for surgical intervention/evacuation: abscess >2.5 cm in diameter (excise or aspirate); any ring-enhancing lesion accessible for diagnostic aspiration; failure to improve/decreasing size on medical therapy alone; significant mass effect/impending herniation; multiloculated abscess; abscess adjacent to the ventricular system (risk of rupture).
d) Indications for MRSA and Pseudomonas coverage: MRSA - penetrating trauma, post-neurosurgical infection, known MRSA colonization/infection, or S. aureus suspected on Gram stain; Pseudomonas - post-neurosurgical/trauma in a patient at risk (nosocomial exposure), immunocompromised host, or known Pseudomonas colonization (use ceftazidime or cefepime).
e) Organisms causing concurrent brain and lung abscess with treatment: Nocardia species (treat with high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole +/- a carbapenem, e.g., meropenem, based on susceptibility) and Actinomyces species (treat with high-dose penicillin G for a prolonged course).

questions.question:
Q16 (2008) Brain abscess
MRI of large abscess in a young man post dental procedure presenting acutely unwell

parts.text: What is the diagnosis
What investigations are needed
Two common sites of metastasis

cohort_answer.text:
Diagnosis: Odontogenic brain abscess (per subsequent slide heading 'Odotogenic brain abscess').
Investigations: Blood cultures, Echo, Dental exam/Panorex, HIV test, CXR.
Two common sites of metastases: Endocarditis, Liver abscess (for S. anginosus), Empyema, Acute bacterial sialadenitis, Peritonitis.

questions.question: 36 year old previously healthy male had a 9 day episode of self-resolving fever. He was fine for the following 4 days, then developed a headache. Today (4 days later) he came in ER because of a tonic-clonic generalized seizure. His CT-scan reveals a solitary left frontal lobe abscess 30x40x20 mm (2014; 2017; 2019)

parts.text: Given the location of this lesion, what is the most likely primary site of infection?
What would be your empirical treatment?

An abscess aspiration reveals abundant neutrophils and gram positive cocci. In anaerobic and aerobic cultures, pinpoint colonies of microaerophilic gram positive cocci in chains are found. Name the group of organism this pathogen belongs to. List 3 members (genus and species) belonging to this group

cohort_answer.text: Primary site: Frontal or ethmoid sinuses. Brain abscess: haematogenous (usually multiple) or direct spread (usually single abscess), post NSx procedure, foreign body, facial trauma. Empiric treatment: CTX 2g IV q12hr (meningeal dosing) + vanco + metro. Organism group: S. anginosus group. Members: S. anginosus; S. intermedius; S. constellatus.

questions.question: A man develops 9 days of fever, which subsides. Then he presents with a tonic-clonic seizure and imaging shows a large frontal lobe abscess.

parts.text: What is the most likely site of origin for this infection?
What is an appropriate antibiotic regimen?
The abscess is aspirated, and grows GPC in chains. They are minute colonies on blood agar that are microaerophilic. What is the most likely group?
Name 3 species within this group.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely site of origin for a frontal lobe abscess: paranasal sinuses (frontoethmoid/frontal sinusitis), spreading via retrograde thrombophlebitis of emissary veins or direct extension.
b) Appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen: metronidazole + a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), adding vancomycin if MRSA is a concern.
c) Gram-positive cocci in chains, minute/pinpoint colonies, microaerophilic: Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group.
d) 3 species within this group: Streptococcus anginosus, Streptococcus constellatus, Streptococcus intermedius.

questions.question: Shortest duration for

parts.text: Cellulitis
Acute uncomplicated pyelo
Peritonsillar abscess (adult: CAP)
VAP
Frontal brain abscess

questions.model_answer: Shortest recommended durations: Cellulitis - 5 days; Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis - 5-7 days (e.g., with a fluoroquinolone); Peritonsillar abscess (comparable to adult CAP context) - 5-7 days after drainage; Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) - 7 days; Frontal (bacterial) brain abscess - typically 4-6 weeks of IV therapy (shortest end of the accepted range), longer than the other listed infections given the difficulty of source control and CNS penetration requirements.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA duration-of-therapy guidance for cellulitis, pyelonephritis, and VAP is not covered in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: Brain Abscess: A young man has a few days of fever and then develops a seizure. Brain imaging demonstrates a 5 cm frontal lobe abscess.

parts.text: A) What is the most likely source of this abscess?
B) What is your empiric therapy?
C) Culture demonstrates pin-point colonies that grow under micraerophilic conditions; GPC on Gram. What is the likely group of organisms?
D) What are the three main members of this group?

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely source: paranasal sinuses (frontal/frontoethmoid sinusitis).
b) Empiric therapy: metronidazole + third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime), +/- vancomycin if MRSA suspected.
c) Pinpoint, microaerophilic GPC: Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group.
d) 3 main members: Streptococcus anginosus, Streptococcus constellatus, Streptococcus intermedius.

questions.question: 23. A young man has a few days fever then develops seizure. Brain image shows 5 cm abscess in frontal lobe.

What is a good empiric choice?

cohort_answer.text: Source: Oral OR paranasal sinusitis. Empiric choice: Ceftriaxone + Flagyl. Organism: S. anginosus. Species in group: S. anginosus, S. intermedius, S. constellatus.

questions.question: Young man (30), otherwise healthy, with frontal lobe cerebral abscess. Had a seizure.

What is the group?
What are the 3 organisms in the group?

b) Group: Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group.

questions.question:
Q15 (2014, 2017 AM) Brain abscess
Man in his 30s presenting with fever and found to have a frontal lobe brain abscess. Drains and shows small microaerophilic colonies on blood agar

parts.text: A) What is the most likely source of infection
B) Empiric Rx
C) Most likely group of causative organisms
D) List 3 members of the group

cohort_answer.text:
A) Odontogenic. Others: hematogenous, direct invasion (post-neurosurgical, penetrating trauma, spread from meningitis/encephalitis, frontal or ethmoid sinuses), subacute and chronic otitis media and mastoiditis.

B) CTX 2g IV q12h + Metronidazole 500mg PO Q6-8h (CNS dosing).

C/D) Streptococcus anginosus group: S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. anginosus.

questions.question:
Q17 (2011 PM) Brain + Lung lesions
AML patient presenting with dyspnea and R sided weakness. Cavitary lung lesions and one brain lesion
Alternate wording: SLE patient on cyclophosphamide and prednisone. Develops lung nodules and brain abscess. List 3 organisms and their tx?
List 3 organisms and initial empiric tx?

parts.text: List 3 organisms and initial empiric tx?

cohort_answer.text: Nocardia: TMP/SMX + imipenem/meropenem + amikacin. Aspergillus: Voriconazole. Tuberculosis: INH/RIF/ETH/PYZ + steroids. Cryptococcus neoformans: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine (treatment phase) → Fluconazole (consolidation and suppressive phases). Actinomyces (A. meyeri, odontolyticus, israelii): Penicillin + surgery for CNS. Streptococcus anginosus: Ceftriaxone. S. aureus: Vancomycin.

parts.text: 3 Abx for empiric Rx

cohort_answer.text: TMP-SMX; Carbapenems: Meropenem and Imipenem; Amikacin (avoid in SOT esp with renal compromise).
